planting.note: Direct sow shelled seed once soil has warmed well past the last frost date; this small-seeded heirloom needs a long, hot growing season to fill its pods before fall's first frost.

directions: Sow raw, unroasted seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since the pegs that carry developing pods underground need soft ground to penetrate easily. Carolina Black is a rare African-heritage heirloom, distinguished from ordinary tan-skinned peanuts by its jet-black seed coat and a sweet, rich flavor that is prized by preservationist growers and heirloom seed keepers in the Carolinas and across the Deep South. Pods typically hold two kernels and are slightly larger than a Spanish peanut, so plants respond well to light hilling of loose soil around the base once yellow blooms appear. Because the variety is scarce commercially, growers often treat a first planting as seed increase, saving pods for replanting the following season.
sources: Peanut Grower magazine — heirloom peanut coverage

common_name: McCormack's Green Glaze Collard (Gullah Geechee Heirloom Collard)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'McCormack's Green Glaze'

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring; frost sweetens the leaves as with other collards.

directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. This variety was preserved by the McCormack family and is one of dozens of distinct named greasy-leaf collards documented through the Heirloom Collards Project, a collaboration between Seed Savers Exchange and Southern seed keepers that has traced individual family lines of collards across the Carolinas and Gulf South back for generations. Its rounded, glossy, deeply dentate leaves carry the same waxy sheen found in other 'glaze' collards, giving natural resistance to leaf-chewing pests, and the plant is slow to bolt and holds well through cold snaps without heading. Because it survives today as a small, actively regenerated seed stock rather than a mass-market variety, gardeners who grow it out and save seed are directly helping preserve a piece of African American Southern foodways.

common_name: Missouri Wonder Pole Bean (Heirloom Cornfield Climbing Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; traditionally grown at the base of corn stalks, which the vines climb in place of a trellis, though a pole or fence works just as well in a home garden.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, giving vines a tall pole, fence, or living corn stalk to climb since plants can reach six to eight feet. Missouri Wonder is a traditional cornfield bean from the early twentieth century, grown intercropped with corn so the climbing vine needed no separate support, a companion-planting approach once common across Southern and Midwestern subsistence farms. The thick, slightly curved pods stay stringless and tender while young, making excellent snap beans, while mature seed can be dried for use as a hearty soup bean through winter. It is notably tolerant of heat and garden stress compared with many bush varieties, and steady daily picking keeps the vigorous vines producing over a long harvest window.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center heirloom bean records

common_name: Traveler 76 Tomato (Heat- and Crack-Resistant Arkansas Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant once frost danger passes; in zone 9 it also performs well as a second, late-summer planting for a fall crop, since it keeps setting fruit through high heat that stalls many other tomatoes.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm starting mix and transplant into full sun after frost risk passes; Traveler 76 was released by the University of Arkansas in 1976 as an improved successor to the original 1930s-era Traveler variety, bred specifically to correct that older tomato's tendency to crack in Southern humidity. The determinate plants set uniform, medium-sized, deep-pink globes with a well-balanced, low-acid flavor and skin that resists splitting after summer rains far better than most heirlooms. It shares the same heat-set reliability that makes Arkansas Traveler famous in Gulf Coast gardens, continuing to produce through the punishing midsummer stretch that causes many varieties to drop blossoms, but its firmer, more uniform fruit and improved crack resistance made it a favored market grower's choice across the mid-South.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service

common_name: Carolina Broadleaf Mustard (Disease-Resistant Southern Mustard Green)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or, better in zone 9, from late summer through fall for a winter harvest; the large, wrinkled leaves develop best flavor after cool weather and light frost.

directions: Direct sow a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season. USDA Agricultural Research Service breeders released Carolina Broadleaf in the mid-2010s as a deliberate improvement on the beloved old Florida Broadleaf mustard, developed specifically to resist a strain of bacterial leaf blight that had begun devastating Florida Broadleaf plantings across the South. It keeps the same large, crinkled, deep-green leaves and classic peppery mustard-green flavor gardeners expect, so it substitutes directly into traditional Southern cooking, but its added disease resistance makes it a more dependable choice where blight has become a recurring problem. Harvest young leaves for salads or let plants mature for the bolder-flavored cooking greens central to Southern braises.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service variety release notes

common_name: Ozark Razorback Cowpea (Calico-Seeded Climbing Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed; this vigorous climbing type does best with a trellis or fence to keep vines and pods up off the ground.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis, fence, or tall stakes since Ozark Razorback is a true climbing cowpea rather than the semi-bush habit of most Southern pea varieties. It is an Ozark Mountain heirloom prized for outstanding drought tolerance and the ability to produce reliably on thin, poor soils where richer garden peas struggle. Each dried seed carries a distinctive calico pattern, with mottled color covering roughly half the seed coat, making saved seed easy to identify from season to season. The fresh-shelled peas cook up creamy and richly flavored, similar to a black-eyed pea, and the vigorous vines also work well as a nitrogen-fixing summer cover crop when a section of the garden is resting between plantings.
